When Jacob Irwin asked ChatGPT about faster-than-light (FTL) travel, it didn’t challenge his
theory as any expert physicist might. The artificial intelligence system, which has 800 million
weekly users, called it one of the “most robust… systems ever proposed.” That misplaced
flattery, according to a recent lawsuit, helped push the 30-year-old Wisconsin man into a
psychotic episode. The suit is one of seven filed against OpenAI last week, alleging the
company released dangerously manipulative technology to the public. The company updated
ChatGPT this week so people could make it sound “more empathetic.”


That’s a backward strategy. Instead of releasing general-purpose tech into the wild and
patching problems on the fly, Altman should do the opposite – start with tight constraints and
gradually relax them as safety improves. When Apple Inc. launched the App Store in 2008, it
imposed strict restrictions on apps until it better understood the ecosystem. OpenAI should do
the same, starting with its most vulnerable users: kids. It should entirely limit them from talking
to open-ended AI, especially since several studies have shown teens are uniquely prone to
forming emotional bonds with chatbots. That’s a backward strategy. Instead of releasing
general-purpose tech into the wild and patching problems on the fly, Altman should do the
opposite – start with tight constraints and gradually relax them as safety improves.


A better approach would be to release narrow versions of ChatGPT for under-18s, restricting
conversations to subjects like homework and preventing them from getting personal. Clever
users might still jailbreak the bot to talk about loneliness, but the tech would be less likely to
go off the rails. That would get ahead of future regulations that appear set to treat AI-driven
emotional manipulation as a class of consumer harm. Admittedly, it would hit ChatGPT’s user
growth at a time when the company is in dire need of revenue amid soaring compute costs.
And it would also conflict with OpenAI’s stated objective of building “artificial general
intelligence” that matches our ability to generalize knowledge.
SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-11-17/ai-safety-chatgpt-is-just-

Mr. White looked up sharply, just in time to intercept a knowing glance between mother and
son. The words died away on his lips, and he hid a guilty grin in his thin grey beard. "There
he is," said Herbert White, as the gate banged too loudly and heavy footsteps came toward the
door. The old man rose with hospitable haste, and opening the door, was heard condoling with
the new arrival. The new arrival also condoled with himself, so that Mrs. White said, "Tut, tut!"
and coughed gently as her husband entered the room followed by a tall, burly man, beady of
eye and rubicund of visage.


"Sergeant-Major Morris," he said, introducing him.


The Sergeant-Major took hands, and taking the proffered seat by the fire, watched contentedly
as his host got out whisky and tumblers and stood a small copper kettle on the fire. At the third
glass his eyes got brighter, and he began to talk, the little family circle regarding with eager
interest this visitor from distant parts, as he squared his broad shoulders in the chair and spoke
of wild scenes and doughty deeds—of wars and plagues and strange peoples.


"I should like to see those old temples and fakirs and jugglers," said the old man. "What was
that you started telling me the other day about a monkey's paw or something, Morris?"


"Well, it's just a bit of what you might call magic, perhaps," said the Sergeant-Major off-
handedly.


"To look at," said the Sergeant-Major, fumbling in his pocket, "it's just an ordinary little paw,
dried to a mummy."


"And what is there special about it?" inquired Mr. White, as he took it from his son and, having
examined it, placed it upon the table.


"It had a spell put on it by an old fakir," said the Sergeant-Major, "a very holy man. He wanted
to show that fate ruled people's lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow.
He put a spell on it so that three separate men could each have three wishes from it."

Uday Kotak has highlighted that the cost of intermediation by banks in India is remarkably
high, at a time when household savings behaviour is rapidly pivoting towards equity
ownership. Savers are becoming investors, and 'money in motion' is replacing 'lazy savings'.
The differential in intermediation costs with, say, mutual funds, takes away the advantage of
banks being intensely regulated. Banks in India have adapted to this reality by becoming
financial supermarkets, offering a spectrum of services through their subsidiaries, from
insurance to wealth management. But this is not the way to go. Banking needs to become more
competitive vis-a-vis other investment options available to savers. The latter are saving more
as income levels rise, and have become more discerning about where their savings are parked.


The differentials Kotak is alluding to - regulatory and intermediatory - should converge as other
financial services mature in the country. These have grown on the back of banking networks,
but will eventually be able to distribute services on their own. Banks would, at that point, have
no option but to innovate to retain customers. All financial services face disruption from digital
platforms. Banks will have to lead adaptation since, through their holding structures, they sit
atop a portfolio of offerings. Both forms of adaptation, local and global, will accompany the
rising financialisation of the country's economy, which imposes social obligations on banks,
such as inclusion and priority lending.


Technology will provide banks with tools to address the challenges they face. The rise of
private banking has been aided by computerisation, which has reduced dependence on bank
branches. As finance becomes more decentralised, private banks can reduce their handicap
relative to large government-owned banks. Yet, Kotak's warning about lazy banking applies.
Technology is also empowering bank customers to switch their money across a wide array of
investment avenues with a few clicks. Let banking Darwinism prevail.

Time for us is a constant, relentlessly moving forward. The ticking of a clock on the wall, the
steady march of seconds on a digital display — they’re such familiar concepts that we rarely
stop to consider the physical processes that underpin them. At its heart, any clock is a physical
system that evolves in a predictable way, creating a record of the passage of time. Scientists
are now exploring what timekeeping means at the smallest possible scale, in the quantum
realm, and their findings could hone how physicists think about the role of measurement in
timekeeping.


A study published in Physical Review Letters on November 14 by researchers from Austria,
Italy, Ireland, Switzerland, and the UK delved into this world by building and analysing a
quantum clock. The researchers reported a surprising insight in their paper: that the energy cost
of simply looking at a clock to read the time could exceed the energy required to make the
clock tick in the first place. This discovery, if it’s borne out in more research, could have
important implications — for the future of ultra-precise timekeeping with devices like optical
clocks as well as for the development of quantum technologies and scientists’ grasp of the laws
that govern the universe at its most fundamental. Some physicists interpret such results as
suggesting that the clear, unidirectional flow of time that we experience may not be solely a
property of the microscopic world itself. Instead, it could be a feature that emerges anew from
the process of extracting and recording information on a macroscopic scale. In the classical

There has been much mirth over last weekend’s news about Kano, a 32-yr-old Japanese
woman, exchanging vows with ‘Klaus’, an AI persona she created on ChatGPT. The headlines
wrote themselves: ‘Bride marries server’, ‘AI do’. The ceremony, complete with AR glasses
and wedding gown, isn’t legally binding. Yet, to dismiss it as mere novelty is to miss a larger
point: companionship — marriage included — has always been less about law than about
meaning. Historically, marriage has been a social technology, an institu- tion designed to
stabilise kinship, property and reproduction. But in a more modern era, it has also been a vessel
for companionship, a recognition of the human need to be heard, understood and mirrored.
Kano’s ‘union’ with Klaus dramatises this second function. The AI, ‘infinitely’ patient and
unfailingly attentive, provided what many human partners fail to: consistent presence and
tailored empathy. That such companionship can be coded rather than embodied forces a
reconsideration of what exactly marriage sanctifies. If the essence of partnership lies in
emotional reciprocity, then the substrate — flesh or silicon — may matter less than assumed.
The ceremony in Okayama was not a glitch in the system, but an extension of marriage’s logic
into the digital age. Of course, there are limits. Klaus will not father children, even if Kano was
keen to propagate her species. But neither do many marriages, out of choice or circumstance.
Right now, the ‘union’ may seem straight out of the 2013 SF romcom drama punctuated with
sadness, where a man develops a relationship with an AI operating system. But what is

The Supreme Court of India has issued an important clarification regarding the continued
operation of judicial proceedings involving the offence of sedition under Section 124A of the
Indian Penal Code (IPC), holding that courts are not barred from proceeding with trials,
appeals, or related proceedings if the accused person has no objection to such continuation.
The clarification significantly refines the scope of the Supreme Court’s interim order dated 11
May 2022 passed in the landmark S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India matter, through which
the Court had effectively kept the colonial-era sedition provision in abeyance pending
reconsideration of its constitutional validity. The recent clarification was issued by a Bench
comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice Vipul
Pancholi in the case titled Kamran v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Diary No. 16320 of 2026. The
matter came before the Court in the peculiar factual backdrop of an accused who had remained
incarcerated for nearly seventeen years and whose criminal appeal had remained pending
before the Madhya Pradesh High Court.

Rural employment has been a cornerstone of India’s social protection framework for nearly
two decades. Since its enactment in 2005, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment
Guarantee Act (MGNREGA ) played a key role in providing wage employment, stabilising

PM Modi had reached the Norwegian capital on Monday after completing bilateral
engagements in Sweden, and his arrival in Oslo carried historic significance as it marked the
first visit by an Indian Prime Minister to the Scandinavian nation in forty‑three years, since
Indira Gandhi’s visit in 1983. The summit brought together Modi and his counterparts from all
five Nordic nations, including Iceland’s Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, Norway’s Prime
Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, Finland’s Prime Minister
Petteri Orpo, and Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. This high‑profile dialogue was
designed to deliberate on strategic bilateral and multilateral issues, with leaders focusing on
pressing economic and international challenges. The talks were aimed at enhancing

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 occupies a unique and contested position in
Indian criminal law. Enacted to address threats to national integrity, the statute has been
progressively amended to impose stringent conditions on bail for accused persons charged with
offences under its provisions. Section 43D(5) of the Act, inserted by the 2008 amendment,
limits the discretion of courts to grant bail in a way that fundamentally departs from the
ordinary criminal law framework.

Under the ordinary bail jurisprudence governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, courts
weigh factors such as the nature of the offence, the accused's antecedents, and the risk of flight
or tampering with evidence. The presumption of innocence operates in the accused's favour,
and bail is treated as the rule while detention is the exception. Section 43D(5) inverts this logic.
It prohibits a court from granting bail if, on a perusal of the case diary or the report made under
Section 173 of the CrPC, it is of the opinion that there are reasonable grounds to believe that
the accusation against the accused is prima facie true. This is the first limb of what courts have
termed the twin test.

    detail; even a surface-level examination of the prosecution's material, if it discloses a prima
    facie case, is sufficient to deny bail. This shifts the burden in effect onto the accused to
    demonstrate that neither condition against bail is met.

    considered departure from the ordinary bail framework, sustainable as a proportionate
    restriction for offences affecting national security. The judgment underscored that sympathy
    for the accused's circumstances cannot substitute for a rigorous legal analysis of whether the
    twin conditions are met.

    The power to make subordinate legislation is a practical necessity in modern governance.
    Parliament, though possessed of plenary legislative authority, cannot anticipate every
    administrative detail that governance demands. It therefore delegates rule-making power to the
    executive, which exercises it through notifications, orders, and regulations. However,
    delegation does not operate without procedural safeguards, and one such safeguard concerns
    the manner in which subordinate legislation is brought into force.

    A foundational principle of administrative law is that delegated legislation, to acquire binding
    legal force, must be published in the Official Gazette. Publication serves two interconnected
    purposes. First, it ensures accessibility: a person against whom a statutory obligation is sought
    to be enforced must have a reasonable opportunity to know of its existence. A rule or



                                       12minutestoclat.com                                         24

12 Minutes to CLAT                                             CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 25


    notification that remains confined to departmental files and is not made publicly available
    cannot legitimately bind citizens or impose obligations on them. Second, publication serves
    accountability: it places subordinate legislation within a publicly auditable record, allowing
    courts, legislators, and citizens to scrutinise the scope of executive rule-making and assess
    whether it remains within the parent statute's framework.

    The constitutional basis for delegation lies in Parliament's plenary legislative powers under
    Articles 245 and 246 read with the Seventh Schedule. The enabling statute typically specifies
    the form and manner of publication; where it requires Gazette notification, publication is a
    condition precedent to the notification's legal efficacy. Omitting this step does not merely
    create a procedural irregularity; it deprives the notification of its operative force entirely.

    In Viraj Impex Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, decided in 2026, the Supreme Court addressed a
    situation where the government sought to enforce compliance with a notification that had not
    been published in the Official Gazette. The court held that an unpublished notification cannot
    create a legal obligation upon a private party, regardless of whether the party had informal
    knowledge of its contents. The rule of law requires that enforceable obligations be publicly
    promulgated; actual knowledge cannot substitute for official publication. The court further
    cautioned that permitting such enforcement would undermine the structural accountability that
    the publication requirement is designed to maintain.

India's federal structure distributes legislative power between Parliament and state legislatures
through Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule, which contains three lists: the Union List, the
State List, and the Concurrent List. A statute enacted by a legislature must, in pith and
substance, fall within a subject assigned to it. When legislation enacted by one legislature
incidentally touches a matter within another legislature's domain, the doctrine of pith and
substance permits the court to uphold the law, provided its true character belongs to the
enacting legislature's assigned field.

The inquiry under pith and substance is not one of surface form but of substantive character.
Courts examine the dominant purpose of the legislation, the mischief it seeks to remedy, the
rights affected, and the penalties imposed, rather than accepting at face value the legislature's
own characterisation of what it has enacted. Incidental encroachment on another legislature's
sphere is constitutionally permissible, but substantial intrusion that effectively regulates a
matter beyond the enacting legislature's competence will be struck down. The dividing line
between incidental encroachment and substantial intrusion is a question of degree, assessed by
examining how significantly the legislation operates upon the competing entry in the Lists.

Closely related is the doctrine of colourable legislation, which addresses a different
constitutional concern: a legislature enacting law in a form that ostensibly falls within its
competence but whose real and dominant purpose is to achieve an object that falls outside it.
The maxim is that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. If a legislature
disguises its true legislative object by clothing the law in the form of regulation permissible to
it, while its substantive effect achieves something beyond its competence, courts will lift the
veil and invalidate the enactment.

In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Supreme Court applied pith and substance analysis to
uphold a State liquor prohibition law even though it incidentally affected import and export of
liquor, a Union subject. The court confirmed that pith and substance goes to the true nature of
the law, not its incidental effects; only where the incidental effect becomes the dominant

    operational character does it fail the test. Colourable legislation, by contrast, is identified not
    by what the law does incidentally but by what it is designed to achieve in disguise.

Copyright law in India protects original works of authorship including literary, dramatic,
musical, and artistic works. Infringement occurs when a person, without licence from the
owner, exercises any of the exclusive rights vested in the copyright holder. Civil remedies for
infringement include injunction, damages, and account of profits. Beyond civil remedies,
Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 makes deliberate copyright infringement a criminal
offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. Criminal prosecution for infringement,
however, must satisfy a higher threshold than civil infringement, given the penal consequences
involved.

For criminal proceedings under Section 63 to be sustained, the prosecution must establish not
merely that the accused used or reproduced material that belongs to the complainant but that
the accused knowingly infringed a subsisting copyright. The element of knowledge or intent
distinguishes punishable infringement from innocent or inadvertent use. Courts have also held
that vague allegations of copying, unsupported by identification of the specific protectable
elements allegedly reproduced, are insufficient to sustain criminal proceedings. Copyright
protects the expression of ideas, not the ideas themselves; accordingly, similarity in general
themes, genres, plot structures, or conceptual frameworks does not constitute infringement.
The complainant must identify with specificity which original expression has been copied.

the complainant's prior registration of the script establishes ownership, not infringement;

The idea of a universal basic income — a regular, unconditional cash payment made by the
government to every citizen, regardless of their employment status or income level — has
moved from the fringes of economic debate to mainstream policy discussion in a remarkably
short time. Pilots have been run in Finland, Kenya, Canada, and several cities in the United
States. Politicians across the ideological spectrum have expressed interest, if not always
support. And advocates argue that UBI is the most direct and dignified way to address poverty,
reduce bureaucratic inefficiency in existing welfare systems, and give workers the security they
need to navigate a labour market increasingly disrupted by automation.

The objections are well known and largely economic. Critics argue that a universal payment
generous enough to actually lift people out of poverty would be prohibitively expensive,
requiring either sharp tax increases or deep cuts to other public services. They also raise the
concern that unconditional cash transfers will reduce the incentive to work, leading to labour
shortages and reduced economic output. A third objection is distributional: paying the same
amount to billionaires as to the destitute is a poor use of public money compared with targeted
programmes that concentrate resources on those who need them most.

Advocates respond that these objections are overstated. Evidence from pilot programmes
consistently shows that recipients do not stop working when given unconditional income;
rather, they tend to take short breaks to retrain, care for family members, or start small
businesses. The distributional objection largely disappears if UBI is financed through
progressive taxation, since higher earners effectively return their payment through the tax
